passages.title: The Secret of Crystal Lake
passages.text: Scientists studying Crystal Lake have discovered that its famous clarity is partly due to tiny freshwater mussels. Each mussel filters up to a litre of water a day, removing algae and particles. However, the population has fallen by a third in the last decade, which researchers link to rising water temperatures. Local authorities are now considering limiting boat traffic during the summer months, although some businesses argue that this would damage tourism, the area's main source of income.

passages.title: Quiet Voices
passages.text: Many people assume that introverts dislike other people. In reality, introversion is more about where we get our energy. passages.title: The Glass Swimmers
passages.text: Visitors to Crystal Lake often mistake the shimmering creatures beneath its surface for fish. They are, in fact, glass newts, a rare amphibian found in only three lakes in the world. Their transparent skin allows predators to see straight through them, which, paradoxically, helps them survive: a hungry heron sees only the stones on the lakebed. Yet this disguise has become a weakness. As tourism has grown, sunscreen and soap from swimmers have clouded the water, and in murky conditions the newts lose their advantage. Local volunteers now run 'clean swim' days, asking visitors to rinse off before entering the lake. Numbers have stabilised, though scientists warn it is too early to celebrate.

passages.title: Should Homework Be Banned?
passages.text: Last month our school trialled a homework-free term in Years 7 and 8. Supporters argued that students would sleep better, read more for pleasure and spend more time with their families. The results were mixed. Surveys showed that most students did feel less stressed, and library borrowing went up by a fifth. However, maths teachers reported that weaker students fell further behind without regular practice, while some parents complained that they no longer knew what their children were learning. The head teacher has decided on a compromise: short, optional tasks, with a weekly 'family project' replacing written exercises.

passages.title: The Boy Who Mapped the Stars
passages.text: When fourteen-year-old Tomás moved to a remote village in Chile, he was miserable: there was no cinema, the internet was patchy, and he didn't know a soul. What the village did have, however, was some of the darkest skies on Earth. A retired astronomer next door lent him an old telescope, and within a year Tomás had logged over three hundred observations. Last spring, one of his photographs revealed a faint comet that professional observatories had overlooked. It has since been named after him. 'I used to think I'd moved to the middle of nowhere,' he says. 'Now I know I moved to the middle of everything.'

passages.title: Should Zoos Still Exist?
passages.text: Few topics divide a classroom as quickly as zoos. Critics argue that even the best enclosures can't replace the vast territories that animals such as elephants and polar bears roam in the wild, and that many zoo animals show signs of stress. Supporters counter that modern zoos are no longer mere entertainment: they run breeding programmes for endangered species, fund conservation work abroad, and inspire millions of children to care about wildlife. Some experts suggest a middle way: zoos should stop keeping species that clearly suffer in captivity and focus on those they can genuinely help.

passages.text: Mum signed me up for drum lessons without asking, which I thought was outrageous. For the first month, I practised as little as I could get away with, and my teacher, Mr Okafor, must have noticed, because he stopped giving me exercises and instead asked me to play along to my favourite songs. That changed everything. Suddenly, I was practising for an hour a day without being told. Last night, I played in the school concert, and although I came in too early in one song, nobody seemed to mind. I hate to admit it, but Mum was right.

passages.title: The Library That Travels by Boat
passages.text: Along the rivers of northern Norway, a boat called the Epos has been delivering books to isolated villages since 1963. Each autumn, it sails from village to village carrying around 6,000 books, and its arrival is something of a festival: children come aboard for storytelling sessions, and adults swap news as well as novels. Funding has been threatened several times, but each time local people have campaigned successfully to save it. For many readers, the boat is the only library they have ever known.

passages.title: Why Teenagers Really Need More Sleep
passages.text: Parents often complain that teenagers are lazy because they stay up late and struggle to get up. Scientists, however, say this has little to do with laziness. During puberty, the body starts producing the sleep hormone melatonin about two hours later than in childhood, so many teenagers genuinely don't feel tired until 11 p.m. or later. Yet most still need nine hours' sleep. Some schools that have experimented with a later start have reported better attendance, fewer car accidents among older students and, in some cases, improved exam results.

passages.title: Why Pandas Are Picky Eaters
passages.text: Giant pandas belong to the bear family and have the digestive system of a meat-eater, yet around 99% of their diet is bamboo. Since their bodies extract very little energy from it, they must eat for up to fourteen hours a day, consuming as much as 38 kilograms. This also explains why pandas move slowly and avoid steep slopes: they are saving energy. Scientists believe pandas switched to bamboo millions of years ago because it was plentiful and few other animals competed for it. The downside is that when bamboo forests flower and die, which happens every few decades, pandas can face starvation.

passages.title: The Rise of Esports in Schools
passages.text: A growing number of schools now have esports teams that compete in video-game tournaments, much as they would in football or netball. Supporters say the teams attract students who have never felt at home in traditional sports, and that players develop genuine teamwork, communication and strategic thinking. Coaches also set strict rules: players must keep their grades up and take regular breaks from the screen. Not everyone is convinced, however. Some parents worry that school esports will simply give children another excuse to spend hours gaming, and they question whether it should count as a sport at all.

passages.title: A Message from Mountain Rescue
passages.text: Every summer, our volunteers are called out to help walkers who are lost, injured or simply exhausted. The majority of these incidents could easily have been avoided. Before setting out, always check the weather forecast and tell someone your route and the time you expect to be back. Don't rely on your phone for navigation: batteries drain quickly in the cold, and signal is patchy in the hills. Carry a paper map and compass, and know how to use them. Finally, remember that turning back is not failure. The mountain will still be there next weekend.

notes.mountains are getting smaller: It's a figure of speech about trying again.

passages.title: Inside the Chocolate Factory (a school trip report)
passages.text: Our trip to the Cocoa Works was not quite the Willy Wonka experience some of us had been hoping for; there were no rivers of chocolate, and nobody was turned into a blueberry. Still, it was fascinating. We learned that cocoa beans taste bitter until they are fermented and roasted, and that it takes around 400 beans to make a single kilogram of chocolate. The highlight was designing our own bars, although Zak's chilli-and-marshmallow creation was, let's say, an acquired taste. Each of us left with a bag of samples, most of which didn't survive the coach journey home.

questions.explain: 'Not quite the Willy Wonka experience… Still, it was fascinating.'

questions.explain: 'An acquired taste' politely means few people like it at first.

passages.title: The Teenager Who Cleaned the Ocean
passages.text: At sixteen, Boyan Slat went diving in Greece and found more plastic bags than fish. Rather than shrugging it off, he spent the next two years designing a system that would use ocean currents to collect floating plastic, instead of sending boats to chase it. Many experts dismissed the idea as naïve, and the first prototypes broke apart in rough seas. Undeterred, his team kept redesigning, and their equipment has now removed hundreds of tonnes of rubbish. Slat himself admits the problem is far from solved: the most important step, he says, is stopping plastic reaching the sea in the first place.

a holiday job on a boat

questions.explain: 'Undeterred' = not put off.

questions.explain: 'Stopping plastic reaching the sea in the first place.'

passages.title: How Clever Are Crows?
passages.text: Most people think of crows as noisy pests, but scientists increasingly rank them among the cleverest animals on the planet. New Caledonian crows, for example, bend twigs into hooks to pull insects out of holes in trees – something even chimpanzees rarely manage. In one experiment, crows were shown a narrow tube of water with a treat floating out of reach. Rather than giving up, they dropped stones into the tube until the water rose high enough for them to grab it. Crows also seem to remember faces: researchers who once caught crows while wearing a particular mask found that the birds scolded anyone in that mask for years afterwards, even people who had done nothing wrong.

questions.explain: 'Most people think of crows as noisy pests.'

notes.they're rare and shy: Nothing suggests they are rare or shy.

passages.title: My First Week at Space Camp (blog)
passages.text: I'd been dreaming about Space Camp for ages, so when I finally got there I was slightly disappointed to discover that the first two days were mostly classroom lessons on rocket science. By Wednesday, though, we were strapped into a machine that spins you in three directions at once, which is supposed to show how astronauts feel when a spacecraft tumbles. I lasted forty seconds before begging to stop! The highlight was Friday's mission simulation: my team had to 'land' a shuttle while dealing with a series of surprise emergencies. We crash-landed twice, but on the third attempt we touched down perfectly. Our instructor said that failing in practice is exactly what keeps real astronauts safe.

questions.explain: 'I was slightly disappointed to discover that the first two days were mostly classroom lessons.'

questions.explain: 'I lasted forty seconds before begging to stop!'

questions.explain: 'Failing in practice is exactly what keeps real astronauts safe.'

passages.title: The Volcano That Wouldn't Erupt
passages.text: For this year's science fair, Ruby and her friend Kofi decided to build the biggest baking-soda volcano the school had ever seen. They spent two weekends shaping it out of papier-mâché and painting it a fiery orange. On the morning of the fair, however, nothing happened when they poured in the vinegar – just a sad little fizz. Instead of panicking, the pair turned their stand into an investigation. They tested different amounts of baking soda in front of the judges and worked out that the mixture had been far too weak for such a big volcano. They didn't win first prize, but the judges gave them a special award for 'thinking like real scientists'.

options: to build a volcano in one day
questions.explain: 'The biggest baking-soda volcano the school had ever seen.'

notes.to investigate a failed experiment: That came later, after it failed.

questions.explain: 'Nothing happened… just a sad little fizz.'

options: they stayed calm and tested it
they packed up the stand and went home early
questions.explain: 'Instead of panicking, the pair turned their stand into an investigation.'

questions.q: Why did they get a special award?
options: for building the biggest volcano in the school
questions.explain: 'For thinking like real scientists.'

passages.title: Review: Kingdom of Tides (board game)
passages.text: Kingdom of Tides is a board game for two to five players in which you build harbour towns on islands that slowly sink as the tide rises. The artwork is gorgeous, and the little wooden boats are a joy to handle. The rules, on the other hand, are a bit of a challenge: our group needed nearly an hour to get through the instruction booklet, and we still got several things wrong in our first game. Once we got the hang of it, though, it became our go-to game for rainy afternoons. My only real complaint is that with five players, you can wait a long time for your turn. With three, it's close to perfect.

passages.title: Notice: The Starlight Library Summer Reading Quest
passages.text: This summer, the Starlight Library invites readers aged 8 to 14 to join our Reading Quest. Collect a quest card from the front desk and read any six books between 20 July and 31 August – they can be novels, comics, poetry or non-fiction. After each book, tell a librarian about it in a few sentences and you'll receive a sticker. Readers who complete their card will be invited to a celebration evening with a mystery guest author. Please note that e-books and audiobooks count too, but books read for school homework do not.

questions.explain: 'Collect a quest card from the front desk.'

passages.title: Why Do Some Animals Glow?
passages.text: In the deep ocean, where sunlight never reaches, around three-quarters of animals can make their own light. This ability, known as bioluminescence, is produced by a chemical reaction inside the animal's body. Creatures use it in surprisingly different ways. The anglerfish dangles a glowing lure in front of its mouth to tempt smaller fish closer. Some squid squirt out clouds of glowing ink to confuse attackers while they escape. On land, fireflies flash in particular patterns to attract a partner, and each species has its own code. Scientists are now studying these natural lights in the hope of using them in medicine, for example to make diseased cells easier to see.

passages.title: Wheelchair Basketball Taster Day
passages.text: When our PE teacher announced a wheelchair basketball taster day, a few of us assumed it would be easier than normal basketball. We couldn't have been more wrong. Just pushing the sports chairs in a straight line was exhausting, and turning quickly while bouncing the ball felt impossible at first. Our coach, Amira, who plays for the national under-21 team, made it look effortless. She explained that players are allowed two pushes of the wheels for every bounce of the ball. By the end of the afternoon, my arms were aching, but I'd scored three baskets and had a completely new respect for the sport. Half the class have now asked to start a club.

passages.title: The Girl Who Invented a Smarter Lunchbox
passages.text: Eleven-year-old Priya was fed up with soggy sandwiches. Every day, the cold drink in her lunchbox leaked condensation onto her bread. Rather than complaining, she designed a lunchbox with two separate sections and a thin layer of cork between them, which stopped the cold from spreading. Her first version was too heavy to carry comfortably, so she replaced the plastic frame with bamboo. She entered the design in a national young inventors' competition and came second out of four hundred entries. A small company has since offered to help her make a few hundred to sell at local markets – although Priya insists she'll keep testing it on her own sandwiches first.

passages.title: Email from a Pen Friend in Japan
passages.text: Hi Sam! You asked what school is like here. The biggest difference is probably that we don't have cleaners – the students clean the classrooms, corridors and even the toilets every afternoon! I hated it at first, but now I quite like it, and it means nobody drops litter. Lunch is eaten in our classroom, and we take turns serving it to each other wearing white hats and aprons. After lessons, almost everyone joins a club. I'm in the astronomy club, which meets four times a week, so I don't usually get home before six. Is your school day longer or shorter than mine? Write soon! Haru

questions.explain: 'The biggest difference… the students clean the classrooms.'
